opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a natural sign of maturity. In the early days, say the DARPA Grand Challenge era, autonomous driving really was a full-stack robotics problem. You had small teams of researchers who had to think about everything at once: perception, localization, planning, control, the hardware, the sensors. Nobody knew what the right decomposition was, so you needed people who could reason across the whole system.

As the field matured and companies invested billions, the problem got broken into well-defined modules with clear interfaces. Then you could hire specialists: a perception team that just pushes detection metrics, a prediction team, a planning team, a simulation and infrastructure team. That's how you scale engineering, and it's how you get a product that's reliable enough to put on public roads. So in that sense it's a success story. The research problem turned into an engineering problem.

But there's a cost I think about a lot as someone in robot learning. Once you fix the interfaces between modules, you also fix your assumptions about the problem. Each team optimizes its own local metric, and errors compound across the boundaries in ways no single team owns. A lot of the hardest failure cases live exactly in those gaps, in the interaction between what perception outputs and what planning needs. That's part of why there's been this swing back toward more end-to-end, learning-based approaches, where you try to optimize the whole system against the actual driving objective.

For general-purpose robotics, especially manipulation, I don't think we're at the point where we can modularize like that yet. We don't know the right abstractions. What's the "bounding box" equivalent for folding laundry or cooking? So for us, it's still very much a full-stack problem, and I think the people who'll make progress are the ones who can think across the whole loop, from data and learning all the way down to the physical interaction. Driving shows us where the field might end up, but also warns us not to lock in the decomposition too early.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized teams optimize local metrics within modules, but it does not explain that they had little need to communicate because each only needed to improve its own benchmark.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually a very natural evolution, and in some ways it's the sign of a field maturing. When I was first getting into robotics, autonomous driving really was the canonical full-stack robotics problem. You had to think about perception, localization, prediction, planning, control, and all the systems integration glue in between, and the same small group of people often touched all of it. That was exciting, but it was also a reflection of how early things were. Nobody knew which part was the bottleneck, so everyone had to understand everything.

What happened over the past decade is that the problem got decomposed well enough that the interfaces between modules became fairly stable. Once you have a reasonably agreed-upon representation coming out of perception, say, you can have a team of fifty people just making perception better without needing to coordinate with the planning team every day. That specialization is how you actually ship a product. It's the same thing that happened with operating systems or compilers. You can't build a safety-critical system with a dozen generalists.

The flip side, and this is something I think about a lot from the research side, is that heavy specialization can lock you into an architecture. The modular stack was designed around what we could do in, roughly, 2015. Now with end-to-end learning and foundation models, some of those boundaries are starting to dissolve again. If your organization is structured so that perception and planning are separate kingdoms, it becomes very hard to even try an approach where a single model does both. So you get this tension where the org chart was optimized for the old decomposition, and the technology is pushing toward a new one.

So my view is that the specialization was correct and necessary, but the field is now swinging back a little. The best groups I see keep a core of people who think about the whole system, who can ask whether the decomposition itself is still right, while the specialized teams keep pushing on each piece. And honestly, for general-purpose robotics, which is more where I work, we're still in that early, full-stack phase. We haven't earned the right to specialize yet, because we don't know what the right modules are. Watching how driving went through this transition is a pretty useful preview of what's coming for the rest of robotics.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized teams could improve their own modules with little day-to-day coordination, but it does not say they communicated little because each team only needed to improve its own benchmark.

astra-6.text:
I think that shift is a sign of the field maturing. Early on, autonomous driving was very much a full-stack robotics problem: you had to think about perception, prediction, planning, and control together, because a decision in one part of the system could change what you needed everywhere else.

As the systems become more established, you can define clearer interfaces and have specialized teams go much deeper on individual components. That’s necessary when you’re trying to build something reliable at scale.

But the full-stack problem doesn’t disappear. You still need people who understand how those components interact. A better perception metric doesn’t automatically mean better driving. So I see specialization as a natural progression, but you still have to evaluate success at the level of the whole system.

r001.rationale: The response says clearer interfaces let specialized teams focus deeply on components, but it does not claim teams had little need to communicate or that each only needed to improve its own benchmark. It instead emphasizes cross-component interaction and whole-system evaluation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that shift is a sign of the field maturing. Early on, autonomous driving was very much a full-stack robotics problem: you needed to understand how perception, prediction, planning, and control fit together, because decisions in one part of the system affected everything else.

As the systems and organizations grew, each of those pieces became a substantial engineering discipline. You could have an entire team working on a very specific perception problem. That specialization lets you go much deeper and build more reliable systems.

The challenge is preserving the system-level perspective. A better perception metric doesn’t automatically mean better driving. You still need people who understand how the pieces interact and can connect improvements in individual components to the behavior of the vehicle. So I see specialization as a natural progression, but that broader robotics perspective remains really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says specialization allowed deeper work, but stresses that component teams must preserve a system-level perspective and connect improvements across components. It does not say teams had little need to communicate or only needed to improve their own benchmarks.
